text: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node from the end of the list and return the head.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — n equals one means remove the last node, and if n equals the length, I remove the head. So for one through five with n equals two, I drop the four and get one, two, three, five. Are there any constraints on the size, and is n guaranteed to be within the list?
Up to thirty nodes, at least one. And yes, n is always between one and the length.

Good — I'll lean on that guarantee, and I'll say where. Let me name the difficulty. A singly linked list has no notion of nth from the end. I can only walk forward. So the obvious approach is two passes: count the length, then walk to position length minus n. Is there a follow-up you want, like doing it in one pass?
Yes — can you do it in one pass?

Let me run through the example first, because it shows what I need. One through five, n equals two. The node to remove is the four. But to actually unlink it, I need the node before it — the three. In a singly linked list you can't delete a node you're standing on; you need its predecessor. I'll come back to that — it decides an off-by-one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive one-pass approach would be to push every node pointer into a vector and index into it. That works, but it spends linear space on something that shouldn't need any — and it uses nothing about the list being a list. This problem reminds me of two pointers held at a fixed gap. If I move one pointer ahead by a fixed number of steps and then advance both together, the gap never changes. So when the front one runs off the end, the back one is at a known distance from the end — without ever counting the length. That turns walk to a position I don't know yet into walk until the front pointer hits null, which is a condition I can actually see.

Here's the plan. One: a dummy node before head, with tail and curr both starting there. Two: advance curr by n plus one steps to open the gap. Three: move both together until curr is null, then unlink tail's next. The gap is n plus one, not n. With n, tail would land on the node I want to remove, and I can't delete from there. One extra step puts tail on the predecessor instead. And I need a dummy node. When n equals the length, the node to remove is the head, which has no predecessor at all. The dummy invents one, so removing the head and removing anything in the middle become the same two lines, and returning dummy next handles the head changing for free. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Three things worth flagging. The loop condition is while curr, not while curr next — the second stops a step early, so tail ends one node short and I'd unlink the wrong node. The dummy lives on the stack, and I delete the removed node — unlinking alone leaves it allocated, and a heap dummy with no delete leaks two nodes per call. And advancing curr n plus one steps without a null check is safe: the dummy plus size nodes makes size plus one slots, and since n is at most size, the furthest I go lands exactly on null. That relies on your guarantee; without it, I'd need a null check there.

Let's dry-run the code with one through five and n equals two, expecting one, two, three, five. The row that matters is opening the gap: curr moves three steps while tail stays on the dummy, so the gap is three. After that it stays three — that invariant is the whole algorithm. When curr falls off the end, tail is on node three, and I unlink the four. That matches. Corner cases: a single node returns empty. Two nodes with n two removes the head — the case the dummy exists for. Thirty nodes with n thirty sends curr furthest, exactly onto null. All four hundred sixty-five legal inputs match a reference. Dropping the dummy fails only thirty of them — exactly the head removals — so it's the most dangerous bug: it hides in the case people skip testing by hand.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear in a single pass — curr takes size plus one steps and tail takes size minus n. Space is constant: two pointers and one stack-allocated dummy. I do want to be honest about what one pass bought us, though. The two-pass version is also linear, with the same constant space and about the same number of pointer steps. One pass matters when a second traversal is genuinely expensive, like streaming data you can only read once. Oh, one more thing — the gap is however many steps you need to stop before the target. If the problem were to return the nth node from the end, the gap would be plain n, with no dummy, since nothing gets modified. So: gap n to read, gap n plus one to delete.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You said you can't delete a node you're standing on during Understand, and then the plus one and the dummy both fell out of that one observation instead of being memorized rules. You checked that advancing by n plus one is in bounds and tied it explicitly to the guarantee I gave you — including what you'd add if that guarantee went away. And you noticed the dummy bug is the least likely to fail and therefore the most likely to ship. That's the right instinct about which bugs actually make it to production.
